courseEvidence.name: Personal & Professional Development
courseEvidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
courseEvidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
courseEvidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design
courseEvidence.contribution: Academic writing, research literacy and civic reflection.

courseEvidence.name: Transnational Business Law
courseEvidence.description2: Businesses and entrepreneurs are confronted with legal complexity not only at the domestic level but particularly across divergent legal systems. This course presents a survey of the most essential fields of business law: contracts law, company law, trade law, intellectual property, and dispute resolution. An ultimate aim of the course is to critically examine the impact of globalization and digitization on the development of business law.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies legal frameworks governing cross-border business transactions, combining comparative and international perspectives with practical legal problem-solving. Topics include trade regulation, contracts and international sales, transport and documentary transactions, finance, services, intellectual property, foreign investment and digital commerce. Advisory assignments assess contractual outcomes, risk allocation, intellectual-property protection and e-commerce compliance. A simulated arbitration develops written legal argument and oral advocacy.
courseEvidence.topics: International trade regulation; Comparative and international contract law; International sales; Transport of goods and Incoterms; Documentary transactions; International trade finance; Employment and sale of services; Intellectual-property protection; International commercial dispute resolution; Foreign direct investment; E-commerce and digital economy regulation
courseEvidence.methods: Comparative legal analysis; Application of legal rules to commercial scenarios; Transport-risk allocation analysis; Intellectual-property strategy assessment; E-commerce legal-compliance analysis; Arbitration memorandum drafting and simulated advocacy
courseEvidence.contribution: Cross-border contracts, trade, intellectual property, foreign investment and digital commerce provide substantive transnational business-law analysis.

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Economics
courseEvidence.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
courseEvidence.topics: Supply and demand; Game theory; Rational consumer choice; Individual and market demand; Production and costs; Perfect competition; Aggregate output; Unemployment and inflation; Goods and financial markets; IS-LM model
courseEvidence.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling
courseEvidence.contribution: Consumer/firm incentives, market structure and aggregate economic effects explain behaviour of actors regulated in platform/transnational-business settings; not legal protection itself.

courseEvidence.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
courseEvidence.description2: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces entrepreneurship and core business functions through the development of a startup concept. Students use design thinking to discover customer needs, define a problem, generate and prototype solutions, and construct value propositions and business models. Marketing, finance, operations, human resources and funding inform a coherent business plan and investor pitch. Entrepreneurial cases and a startup simulation examine decision-making, early growth and business lifecycles, with attention to societal impact and sustainability.
courseEvidence.topics: Entrepreneurial mindset and pathways; Business environments, ownership and competition; Customer needs; Value propositions; Business models; Marketing and sales; Finance and accounting; Venture funding; Operations and human resources; Competitive positioning; Startup growth and business lifecycles; Sustainability and societal impact
courseEvidence.methods: Design thinking; Customer-needs discovery; Ideation and prototyping; Value Proposition Canvas; Business Model Canvas; Business planning; SWOT and risk assessment; Startup simulation
courseEvidence.contribution: Venture ideation, market validation and business planning explain how firms formulate transactions and commercial models later examined in transnational/platform-business law; not legal doctrine.

courseEvidence.name: Research Methods & Statistics
courseEvidence.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
courseEvidence.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
courseEvidence.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: Research design, sampling, operationalisation, inference/ANOVA and a group project supply empirical methods for investigating law-related social questions.

courseEvidence.name: Negotiation & Strategic Thinking
courseEvidence.description2: How do you get to yes? In this course you will learn how to craft persuasive arguments, deploy the right language, negotiate more effectively, and influence decisions with confidence—whether in business, leadership, or life.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops negotiation as an analytical practice and interpersonal skill. Students learn interest-based bargaining, BATNA and ZOPA, value creation, framing, concessions and strategies for handling power, emotions and difficult counterparts. Social-psychological and communication perspectives connect negotiation to trust, ethics, culture and relationships. Frequent simulations and narrative analysis lead to an annotated negotiation film and the design, teaching and evaluation of a negotiation scenario grounded in Delta Climate Center themes.
courseEvidence.topics: Interests versus positions; BATNA and ZOPA; Mutual gains and objective criteria; Dual-concern model; Anchoring, framing and concessions; Trade-offs and logrolling; Cognitive biases and influence; Power and emotions; Trust, reputation and ethics; Cross-cultural and organizational negotiation; Negotiation implementation and withdrawal; Stakeholder interests
courseEvidence.methods: BATNA and ZOPA analysis; Stakeholder-interest mapping; Interest-based negotiation; Negotiation simulations; Narrative and film analysis of bargaining; Negotiation-scene scripting and annotation; Scenario design and reflective evaluation
courseEvidence.contribution: BATNA/ZOPA, bargaining structures, trade-offs and negotiation simulations provide dispute-negotiation skills; mediation procedure is not assumed.

courseEvidence.name: AI Ethics
courseEvidence.description2: Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines AI through ethical theory and psychological accounts of human behaviour and interaction. Ethical debates address fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Psychological perspectives consider development, clinical care, social and organizational relationships, forensic applications and cognitive neuroscience. Students synthesize literature and apply ethical frameworks in an analytical psychology project and a research-grounded podcast, with a creative communication component.
courseEvidence.topics: Algorithmic fairness and bias; Privacy and surveillance; Responsibility and accountability; Human-value alignment; Moral status of AI; Existential risk and democratic implications; Trust and agency in human-AI interaction; AI in clinical care; Child development and AI; Social and organizational effects of AI; AI in forensic psychology; Cognitive and socioemotional development; AI consciousness and sentience
courseEvidence.methods: Ethical-framework application; Philosophical argument evaluation; Psychological-literature synthesis; Theory-based analysis of AI applications; Research podcast scripting, recording and editing
courseEvidence.contribution: Studies AI ethics and human interaction, including fairness, privacy and responsibility.

courseEvidence.name: Governance of Sustainability
courseEvidence.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
courseEvidence.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
courseEvidence.topics: Institutions, actors and power; Collective action and common-pool resources; Governance modes and networks; Techno-optimism and ecological limits; Climate justice; Populism and environmental politics; Wicked and long-term problems; Public participation; Food, water and energy governance; Markets, public goods and externalities; Adaptive and global governance; Climate mitigation; Policy effectiveness and feasibility
courseEvidence.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives
courseEvidence.contribution: Rule-making, governmental/nonstate actors, interests and sustainability policy/enforcement supply governance analysis complementary to environmental law; not professional legal ethics.

courseEvidence.name: Climate Change
courseEvidence.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
courseEvidence.topics: Anthropogenic climate change; Greenhouse gases; Feedback loops and tipping points; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Biosphere impacts; Agriculture, transport and construction; Climate and health; Climate justice and governance; Paris Agreement; Renewable energy and sustainable heat; Carbon removal and geoengineering; Climate communication and misinformation; Climate anxiety; Mitigation and adaptation
courseEvidence.methods: Stakeholder interviewing; Short-film production for climate communication; Source-credibility evaluation; What? So What? Now What? reflective model
courseEvidence.contribution: Climate mechanisms, social effects, justice and mitigation establish the factual background for evaluating legal/governance climate responses; not treaty or corporate climate law.

courseEvidence.name: Law, Society & Justice
courseEvidence.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.
courseEvidence.topics: Legal positivism and empirical and normative perspectives; Common-law and civil-law traditions; Constitutional and administrative law; Criminal law; International law and human rights; Property, contract and tort law; Justice; Law and social control; Law and social change; Race and gender in law; Family law
courseEvidence.methods: Legal interpretation; Case-law research and IRAC case briefing; Demand-letter drafting; Mock-trial legal argumentation; Socio-legal research design; Literature review
courseEvidence.contribution: Case law, trial simulations and legal/social/normative perspectives establish the integrated law-and-society foundation.

courseEvidence.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
courseEvidence.description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.
courseEvidence.topics: Human-rights generations and justifications; UDHR and its formation; UN and European human-rights protection; Natural law and natural rights; Legal positivism and cultural relativism; Universality and statelessness; Human dignity; Right to life and reproductive rights; Torture and punishment; Freedom of religion; Freedom of expression; Democracy
courseEvidence.methods: Treaty and legal-text analysis; Judicial and treaty-body case-law research; Case-law analysis; Philosophical text and argument analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: Human-rights treaties, monitoring/case law and natural-law philosophy connect legal protection to justice and ethical argument.

courseEvidence.name: Criminal Law & Criminal Justice
courseEvidence.description2: Examines moral and legal justifications for criminalisation and punishment. Investigates guiding principles of criminal law and justice, including criminal accountability, guilt, legality and fundamental principles, and applies theory through a simulated legal aid clinic.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines the principles of criminal liability and the legal and moral bases of criminal justice. Students study criminal acts, causation and mental elements, legality, punishment, criminalization, justifications, excuses, inchoate offences and participation. A simulated legal-aid clinic applies doctrine to hypothetical facts through advice memoranda and oral argument. A criminology or organized-crime research proposal develops a literature review and methodology.
courseEvidence.topics: Criminal accountability; Actus reus and causation; Intent, recklessness and negligence; Legality and presumption of innocence; Theories of punishment; Criminalization and its limits; Justifications and excuses; Preparation and attempt; Participation in crime; Corporate criminal liability; Criminology and organized crime
courseEvidence.methods: Comparative criminal-law analysis; Case-law analysis; Application of legal principles to hypothetical facts; Legal-advice memorandum writing; Simulated legal-aid argumentation; Criminological research design and literature review
courseEvidence.contribution: Criminal accountability, guilt, legality, punishment and simulated legal advice implement substantive criminal-law reasoning; criminological causation remains limited.

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Public International Law
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces rules, institutions and politics of public international law. Covers treaties, the UN, armed conflict, war crimes, refugee protection and climate change. Students analyse cases, debate issues and produce a podcast connecting law to global challenges.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces public international law through its sources, theories, institutions and relationship to domestic legal systems. Legal principles are applied to responsibility, force, armed conflict, international crime, human rights, economic relations and environmental protection. The later course examines self-determination, Third World approaches, soft law, compliance and treaty politics. Case exercises develop legal reasoning, while a research podcast critically investigates a political dimension of international law.
courseEvidence.topics: Sources and theories of international law; Treaty law; International legal subjects; Jurisdiction and immunities; Domestic courts and international law; State responsibility; Use of force; UN reform; Armed conflict and international criminal law; International human rights and economic law; Environmental law; Self-determination; Third World Approaches to International Law; Soft law, compliance and effectiveness; Global environmental treaties
courseEvidence.methods: Identification and interpretation of international legal instruments; Judgment and case-law analysis; Application of legal principles to factual scenarios; Legal, empirical and normative critique; Research podcast development
courseEvidence.contribution: Examines sources and institutions of public international law, including human rights, responsibility, force and environmental protection.

courseEvidence.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
courseEvidence.description2: Explores constitutional law and state organisation, using a comparative approach. Covers constitutionalism, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism and fundamental rights, and discusses constitution‑making, religious constitutions and constitutional backsliding.
courseEvidence.profile: Compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. Students examine constitutional features, federalism, legislatures, executive relationships, courts, judicial review and human rights. The administrative component addresses public participation, remedies and procedural fairness. A staged booklet compares two constitutions, supported by legal interpretation, case-law analysis and application of principles to hypothetical facts.
courseEvidence.topics: Constitutional origins and fundamental features; Federalism and decentralization; Parliaments and lawmaking; Governments and heads of state; Court systems and judicial review; Constitutional rights; EU constitutional order; Administrative-law functions; Public participation; Administrative remedies; Procedural fairness, discretion and legitimate expectations
courseEvidence.methods: Comparative constitutional analysis; Constitutional and legislative interpretation; Case-law analysis; Application of legal principles to hypothetical facts; Structured comparative legal writing
courseEvidence.contribution: Comparative constitutional/administrative principles, state power and rights supply public-law reasoning across legal systems.

courseEvidence.name: Principles of Private Law
courseEvidence.description2: Examines principles of property law, tort law, contract law and other fields within private law. Uses comparisons of legal systems in four countries to explore rights and obligations arising from daily interactions.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines property, tort and contract law through comparison of legal systems, primarily Germany, France, England, China and the United States. Students analyze rights and obligations, ownership, nuisance, negligence, contract formation and fairness, remedies and related policy pressures. Legal issue briefs apply the IRAC method. An issue-based comparative contract-law paper and simulated mediation develop comparative analysis, legal argument and negotiation.
courseEvidence.topics: Possession and ownership; Nuisance and property restrictions; Easements, covenants and servitudes; Necessity; Tort structure, intent and negligence; Duties to act; Offer and acceptance; Pre-contractual liability and mistake; Contract fairness and excuse; Specific performance and damages; Unjust enrichment; Mediation and dispute resolution; Private law and public policy
courseEvidence.methods: Functional comparative legal analysis; IRAC legal briefing; Case-law analysis; Application of doctrine to hypothetical facts; Comparative contract-law research; Mediation-position drafting; Simulated mediation and negotiation
courseEvidence.contribution: Comparative property, tort and contract principles and their social pressures supply the private-law strand of the legal response.

courseEvidence.name: Foundations of European Union Law
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces the EU legal order through its institutions, sources, competences and relationship to member-state law. Students study supremacy, legal effect, liability and judicial remedies before applying citizenship and free-movement law to concrete problems. Structured legal cases and research into current judgments develop interpretation and comparison across EU and domestic settings. Digital regulation and the green transition provide a contemporary application.
courseEvidence.topics: European integration and institutions; EU legal sources and fundamental rights; Competences, subsidiarity and proportionality; Supremacy; Direct and indirect effect; State liability; Preliminary rulings; Review of EU acts and enforcement; EU citizenship; Free movement of persons, workers and goods; Establishment and services; Digital-market regulation and green transition
courseEvidence.methods: EU legal-source research; Case-law analysis; Comparative interpretation of EU and national law; Application of free-movement principles to factual scenarios; Structured legal problem analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: EU legal institutions, rights, citizenship and free movement analysed through cases/PBL supply the multilevel European-law strand.

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces major philosophical questions through close study of arguments from ancient Greek thought to contemporary philosophy, with a related Buddhist perspective on the self. Students examine knowledge, ethics, God, mind and consciousness, freedom, identity, time and meaning. Historical texts and contemporary debates, including AI consciousness and concepts of race and gender, develop the ability to reconstruct, evaluate and formulate philosophical arguments in focused essays.
courseEvidence.topics: Knowledge, opinion and scepticism; Virtue, duty and consequentialist ethics; Moral objectivity; Existence of God; Idealism and causation; Mind-body problem and consciousness; AI and consciousness; Free will and responsibility; Personal identity and non-self; Existentialism; Race and gender; Time; Meaning of life
courseEvidence.methods: Close reading of philosophical texts; Conceptual analysis; Philosophical argument reconstruction and evaluation; Argumentative essay development
courseEvidence.contribution: Theoretical tools, knowledge, responsibility and rigorous argumentation support reflective legal/normative reasoning; not a dedicated philosophy-of-law course.

courseEvidence.name: Theory of International Relations
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces basic theories of international relations and applies them to contemporary issues such as climate change, energy, humanitarian intervention, global crises and international relations between North-South and South-South actors. Includes a UN Security Council negotiation simulation.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces international relations and geopolitics through competing theoretical approaches and historical and contemporary cases. Students study realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism, critical theory and foreign-policy analysis. Case research connects theories to conflicts, colonial relationships, economic competition and climate politics. A UN Security Council simulation requires country-position research, strategy and position papers, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.
courseEvidence.topics: International state system and non-state actors; Classical and contemporary geopolitics; Realism and neorealism; Liberalism and neoliberalism; Marxism and world-systems theory; Constructivism and critical theory; Foreign-policy decision-making; War and great-power competition; Colonialism and economic relations; Climate politics; UN Security Council diplomacy
courseEvidence.methods: Theory-guided international case analysis; Historical-source analysis; Comparative foreign-policy analysis; Country-position and strategy research; Diplomatic negotiation simulation; Position-paper and resolution drafting
courseEvidence.contribution: Compares international relations theories and applies them to global political and institutional cases.

courseEvidence.name: European Union Politics
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
courseEvidence.topics: European integration; EU institutions and decision rules; EU legitimacy and democracy; Public opinion; Parties and European Parliament; Interest representation and lobbying; Agenda setting; EU legislation and implementation; MEP roles and committee behaviour; Political ideology and amendments; Policy salience
courseEvidence.methods: EU policy and legislative-document research; Process tracing; Systematic amendment coding; Ideology and amendment-activity analysis; Salience assessment; Comparative news-source analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: EU institutions, legislative dossiers and organised-interest research explain the political process through which legal rules and economic policies are formed.

courseEvidence.name: Peace & Conflict
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces Peace & Conflict Studies. Examines definitions of peace and conflict; analyzes conflict causation, violence typologies and radicalisation; applies reconciliation and conflict‑transformation models to real‑world scenarios through lectures and portfolio work.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines causes and dynamics of conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies are connected to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. Students compare travelling concepts across disciplines, produce an interdisciplinary podcast, and develop an evidence-based policy brief with a research dossier. Positionality reflection addresses how assumptions shape inquiry.
courseEvidence.topics: Conflict theories and structural violence; Identity and historical grievances; Colonialism and forced migration; International peace and security; Humanitarian law and human rights; Positive, negative and hybrid peace; Local peacebuilding; Frozen conflicts; Counterterrorism and rule of law; Transitional justice; Gender and conflict; Development and peacebuilding; Reconciliation, arts and religion; Global South perspectives; Travelling concepts and researcher positionality
courseEvidence.methods: Interdisciplinary Research Process; Cross-disciplinary travelling-concept analysis; Conflict case analysis; Context and stakeholder mapping; Annotated bibliography and evidence synthesis; Policy-option appraisal; Policy-brief and background-dossier development; Researcher positionality analysis; Comparative research podcast production
courseEvidence.contribution: Conflict causes, violence, structural inequality and peacebuilding/reconciliation explain social problems addressed by security and justice institutions; not criminal doctrine.

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Sociology
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
courseEvidence.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
courseEvidence.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation
courseEvidence.contribution: Sociological theories and institutions, race/gender and colonial contexts provide a social explanation of the settings in which law operates.

courseEvidence.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
courseEvidence.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
courseEvidence.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation
courseEvidence.contribution: Research design, interviews/meaning, data interpretation and reflexivity supply qualitative methods before later applied empirical work.

courseEvidence.name: Social Psychology
courseEvidence.description2: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.
courseEvidence.topics: Social cognition and person perception; The self and self-motives; Social influence; Persuasion, attitudes and behaviour; Group processes; Prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination; Prejudice reduction; Interpersonal aggression; Prosocial behaviour; Interpersonal attraction and close relationships
courseEvidence.methods: Critical appraisal of empirical social-psychology research; Literature synthesis; Theory-guided hypothesis formulation; Research design for a proposed social-psychology study
courseEvidence.contribution: Social influences on judgments, attitudes and behaviour supply the psychological perspective needed to interpret legal actors and public responses.

courseEvidence.name: Youth Resilience to Extremism
courseEvidence.description2: Interdisciplinary course combining psychology and other social sciences in which students will have an opportunity to participate in an actual international research project and develop evidence-based materials for youth leaders and educators aimed at strengthening young people’s resilience to radicalization by promoting democratic school culture, emotionally supportive learning environments, empathy, civic engagement, and mental well-being.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines youth radicalization and educational prevention through psychology, education, sociology, political science and peace education. Models of radicalization and adolescent risk and protective factors lead into inclusive school climates, belonging, social-emotional learning, dialogue, media literacy and civic agency. Students translate primary research into teacher-training materials and a youth toolkit for an international school project, then revise the resources using feedback from intended recipients.
courseEvidence.topics: Radicalization, violent extremism and terrorism; Developmental and psychosocial pathways; Risk and protective factors; School climate and belonging; Identity and peer influence; Social-emotional learning and well-being; Empathy and perspective-taking; Conflict resolution and intercultural dialogue; Mental-health literacy and referral; Digital literacy and misinformation; Youth leadership and democratic participation; Counter- and alternative narratives
courseEvidence.methods: Primary-research synthesis; Intervention-evidence appraisal; Case and classroom-scenario analysis; Inclusive educational-resource design; Alternative-narrative development; Recipient-feedback collection and iterative revision; Ethical appraisal of prevention tools
courseEvidence.contribution: Uses research on youth radicalisation, risk and protective factors to inform educational prevention.

comparability.assessment: The legal and social research option combines eight legal courses with quantitative and qualitative research, sociology, psychology, negotiation and international governance. Environmental science and business courses give the legal questions context. A separate sustainability and markets option can study policy, firms and environmental impacts, but lacks a distinct sequence in platform regulation, climate law or evaluation of legal interventions. Adding the same legal core would repeat the primary option without establishing a separate legal focus.

repair: Criminal Law & Criminal Justice moves to the fifth term and Introduction to Economics to the first. Western Philosophy and Introduction to Sociology exchange those slots. All 24 courses are retained. Eight legal courses give substantive coverage across law fields, while sociological and psychological inquiry, qualitative and quantitative research, negotiation and governance apply related methods. International and EU law include human rights, treaty law and free movement, alongside national and international institutions. An alternative with environmental and market companion courses can add policy, life-cycle, accounting and digital market analysis. These additions cannot form a second substantive legal sequence in environmental liability, platform work, remedies or legal evaluation. A separate security or migration route would likewise rearrange the existing legal core without a sustained specialist sequence. The retained route makes these interests visible as partial overlaps and limits.
alignments: Security, criminal justice and legal philosophy

VU studies defamation and assault as specific legal problems.
VU examines diversity within the programme’s legal and social context.
Both develop empirical research design and statistical reasoning. UCR applies these skills in a group research project.
Both connect law to philosophical questions about rights and justice. UCR concentrates on human-rights law and its foundations.
Both use psychology to explain behaviour. UCR focuses on social influence, attitudes and group processes.
